1:
Keil and Delitzsch count the refrain twenty-six times as an intercalary verse, call the psalm the great Hallel by pre-eminence, and report three opinions in the Talmud and Midrash on the compass of that title. They find song and counter-song in six-line strophes as far as the eighteenth verse and eight-line strophes after it, from the point where dependence on the preceding psalm turns into borrowing. Adam Clarke calls the psalm little else than a repetition of the one before, takes it for a responsive song, the Levites singing the verse and the people the burden, and notes that it has no title in the Hebrew or in any version and was written after the captivity. John Calvin quotes a writer who finds the artifice characteristic of the captivity and restoration while allowing it earlier, and who argues that poetry everywhere comes in time to lean less on exactness of arrangement and more on external contrivance — metre, rhyme, assonance, a recurring burden — probably ordained to help the memory of a people cut off at Babylon from public teaching. Calvin defends the repetition by noting that choruses are allowed and admired in profane poets.

The plural titles divide them. John Gill follows Aben Ezra and Kimchi in taking the gods for angels, whose God is Christ, and adds that the heathen called the Maker of all things the God of gods, a title they gave to Janus. Clarke rules out idols, since God is not their god, and applies one title to priests and the other to magistrates. John Wesley admits all three, angels, princes and idols; Matthew Henry takes them at once, the God whom angels adore, from whom magistrates derive their power, and by whom all pretended deities shall be conquered. Calvin will not settle the referents, and makes the plural a concession to the tendency in men to divide the Godhead and delight in a multiplicity of gods, the word intimating that the fullest perfection of dominion is in the one God.

Charles Ellicott watches the poet handle the creation account: it recalls the older one but takes its words elsewhere, the verb for stretching out being peculiar to one prophet and to this psalm, properly to beat out with the feet and then to overlay with metal, so that the earth becomes a plate spread upon the waters where the older account has it emerge from them; and the word for lights means light itself, not luminaries. Clarke reads the same clause of a central abyss of waters whose existence has not yet been disproved, and defines the wonders as the suspension of the laws of nature. Henry warns that the lights are called great because they appear so to us, astronomers knowing the moon smaller than many stars but nearer, and adds that they rule because benefactors are the best rulers, so the powers the Gentiles idolized are servants.

Augustine of Hippo presses the hardest question here. If after the judgment the just are in life eternal and the unjust in everlasting fire, none is left for God to pity; how then is the mercy for ever? His answer is that the blessedness mercifully bestowed, by which the miserable cease to be miserable, itself has no end, so that to become just from unjust, alive from dead and happy from wretched is of a mercy that lasts. Clarke would render the burden as saying the tender mercy is to the coming age, and takes it, if the psalm is prophetic, of the redemption of the world. Henry asks that thanks be given not because God does good but because he is good, the streams traced up to the fountain, and remarks that we are never so earnestly called upon to pray or repent as to give thanks, that being the work of heaven; Spurgeon hears the exhortation pleaded with an O three times repeated.
10:
The refrain becomes a problem here, and Charles Ellicott is the one who says so: after the destruction of the firstborn, and again after war and slaughter, the words sound harsh to Christian ears. His answer is philological — the word rendered mercy carries the sense of covenant grace, a special favour of God in which the heathen did not share and which was often most signally shown in their destruction. The others meet the same difficulty by other routes. John Gill finds justice in the stroke, since Egypt had used the Lord’s firstborn ill and slain their sons, and finds mercy in it too, and observes that the blow fell on a tender part, on sons and heirs who were to inherit the estates and perpetuate the names. C.H. Spurgeon allows that judgment is God’s strange work but holds that when mercy to men demands severe punishment he will not hold back his hand from the needful surgery; the last plague struck all Egypt to the heart, from king to slave each wounded in the tenderest point, the joy and hope of every household struck down in a moment, and justice, which had lingered, struck home at last. Matthew Henry makes the sea itself a miracle of justice as well as of mercy, the same water being a lane to the Israelites and a grave to their pursuers, and notes that of all the plagues only this one is named because it was the conquering plague. Adam Clarke simply counts the cost: a great part of the rising generation was cut off, and few but old persons and children were left remaining.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the hinge. Up to this point the psalm has praised God the absolute, the Creator of all things; from here onwards it praises the God of the history of salvation. They notice also that the verb used for dividing the sea is not the one the older narratives and another psalm employ.

The dividing itself carries a tradition that two of them stop to refuse. Gill reports it from Jarchi, Kimchi and Arama — that the sea was parted into twelve, a path apiece for the twelve tribes — and answers that for this there is no foundation, holding to two parts with the waters standing as a wall on either hand and the whole done by a strong east wind. Clarke reports the same imagination among the Jews, adds that many of the fathers were of the same opinion, and asks whether it is very likely. Neither will spend more than a sentence on it, and both keep the two walls.

Gill reads the whole passage twice over. The strong hand and stretched-out arm are the power that brought Israel out and the power by which the mystical Israel is redeemed from enemies stronger than itself; the passage through the sea is the making of a people willing and courageous, so that not one was lost in the crossing, and the figure of afflictions passed through with everlasting arms underneath; the overthrow in the same water is an emblem of the destruction of Satan and his principalities, and of the casting of the sins of God’s people into the depths of the sea, never to appear again to their condemnation. Henry works the same ground historically rather than typically: the miracles proved the commission of Moses to give Israel a law and laid the nation under lasting obligation to obey it, and God not only divided the sea but gave the people courage to go through it when it was divided, which was a power over men’s hearts as the dividing was a power over the waters. Spurgeon keeps the wider frame, that the design was mercy to Israel and through Israel to succeeding ages and to all the world.
16:
The wilderness draws out C.H. Spurgeon at length and almost nobody else. He begins from the logic of it: God led them into the wilderness and was therefore pledged to lead them through, and the wilderness itself was to remain as barren as ever. The people knew nothing of the way but were led; they were a vast host, yet all of them were led; there were neither roads nor tracks, and being led by unerring wisdom they never lost their way. He names the means — Moses, Aaron, Jethro, the pillar of cloud — and observes that their feet did not swell nor their garments wear out in all the journey, and that their own conduct tested the mercy most severely but it bore the strain. Adam Clarke makes the same point as a sum: it was an astonishing miracle to support so many hundreds of thousands in a wilderness totally deprived of all necessaries for the life of man, and that for forty years. John Gill keeps to the plain fact that there was no path, and that the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night showed them which way to go.

On the kings Gill weighs two identifications. The great kings may be the thirty-one kings of the land, or they may be the two named in the following verses; he prefers the second, on the ground that the kings of the land were petty kings while these were greater ones. He adds that the famous kings were famous for power, strength, courage and valour, and that they were not merely smitten and discomfited but slain in battle; that the people of the first were strong and warlike; that the country of the second was large and fruitful and its king of gigantic stature; and that the land was taken from those who served idols and given to a people who served the true God, which he calls a reward to servants in a way of grace and not of debt.

Charles Ellicott stops at a single letter. The name of the first king is preceded by a preposition, so that the line reads literally to Sihon; he judges that the composer, having begun so many verses with that preposition, set it here inadvertently, and that the slip was then copied into the parallel verse of the neighbouring psalm. John Wesley notices that the nation is spoken of as though it were one man, and explains that they were united together in one body in the worship of God.
23:
Whose low estate is it? John Gill lays out the options without hiding the last of them: Jarchi takes it of the bondage in Egypt, others of the times of the Judges when God raised up one deliverer after another, and Aben Ezra and Kimchi of the Babylonian captivity, the last of these preferring the captivity of his own people in his own day — to which Gill answers that as yet they are not remembered in a gracious way and manner. Adam Clarke settles for Babylon, reading the verse as a congregation saying that God did much for our forefathers and much for us, delivering us when we had no helper. Matthew Henry takes the many redemptions out of the hands of oppressors, the judges and at length David, as types of the one redemption of the universal church, and presses the point that the Son was sent to redeem us and not the angels that sinned. C.H. Spurgeon makes it wholly personal: ours was an estate of bankruptcy and mendicancy, once so low as to be at hell’s mouth, and if the Lord could have changed towards any it would have been towards us who have brought ourselves low, kept ourselves low, and prepared ourselves to sink yet lower.

Charles Ellicott sharpens the next verse by a word: not redeemed but snatched us from, the verb used elsewhere of a lion seizing his prey. He then raises and refuses the widest reading of the psalm. At the giving of food to all flesh the mercy appears to take a wider range and to reach all men — but only apparently so, since Israel could think of God providing for the bodily wants of everyone because he was the creator of everyone, while the covenant grace remained theirs alone. Spurgeon goes the other way, calling it a boundless mercy that knows no limit from the meanness of its object, reaching down even to beasts and reptiles, and argues that because the Lord feeds all life he may be expected to take special care of his own family. Henry finds it an instance of providence that wherever God has given life he gives food agreeable and sufficient, and calls him a good housekeeper who provides for so large a family. Clarke is struck less by the quantity than by the fitting: the appointing to every living thing the food suited to its nature, the natures being endlessly diversified, he takes for an overwhelming proof of providence. Gill spreads it over Jews and Gentiles, good men and bad, and adds spiritual food for those who are flesh of Christ’s flesh. John Wesley gives the reason for putting the verse in a hymn at all: the psalmist teaches us to render these praises on the creatures’ behalf, because those most concerned in them either cannot or do not perform the duty.

Two of them notice that the psalm does not end where it ends. Clarke reports that the Vulgate, the Arabic and the Anglo-Saxon add a twenty-seventh verse by repeating the third, and calls it very unnecessary; Ellicott notes the same repetition at the close and refers the reader to the Prayer Book, without complaint. Ellicott has one more historical remark for the closing title: God of heaven was not used before the exile, though implied earlier, and away from Zion and the visible token of the divine presence the hearts of the faithful began to think of their God as one whose mansion is on high above the reach of mortal eye. Gill takes the same title of the maker and possessor of heaven, where the inheritance is reserved; Spurgeon of a throne set in glory out of reach of foes, whose glory angels proclaim in every heavenly street; Henry of the great benefactor, from whom every good gift comes down, so that every stream is traced to the fountain.
